newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 24.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- BRITAIN 'LEADS WAY IN EUROPE'

A new Trade Advisory Board created by the British branch of the American Chamber of Commerce, claims that Britain offers the best prospects for economic growth and investment in the European Union because of a "mental gridlock" inside other parts of Europe. The board says Europe needs the "Thatcher factor" to shake-up its thinking and policies. It also says business has a disinclination to invest or increase jobs on the Continent because of high tax burdens, heavy social bills and other obstacles.
-- ADT SEEKING 50 MILLION DOLLARS IN DAMAGES

The security and vehicle auction business, ADT, is to challenge Chase Manhattan Bank in a New York courtroom over its role in a 3.5 billion dollar hostile bid from Western Resources. ADT is to allege that Chase, which lent ADT 500 million dollars in 1993, used confidential information about the company in providing financing and advice for Western's attempted takeover. ADT is seeking a preliminary injunction to prevent Chase from helping Western, plus 50 million dollars in damages.
-- MASTERCARD TAKES CONTROL OF MONDEX

American credit and debit card group, Mastercard, has taken majority control of Mondex International, one of the pioneers of electronic smartcards. The deal will accelerate the expansion around the world of the smartcards, which can be used instead of cash for shopping, phone calls and travel. Mastercard will take a 51 percent stake in Mondex, with the other 49 percent staying with founding organisations, including NatWest, Midland Bank and its HSBC parent, plus Barclay's American subsidiary, Wells Fargo.
THE TIMES
-- LME CHIEF TO BE QUESTIONED OVER SUMITOMO STATEMENT

Chief executive of the London Metal Exchange, David King, is to face questions over whether he breached the Financial Services Act when he was trying to calm markets over the Sumitomo scandal. Labour's Shadow Secretary, Mike O'Brian, is set to raise the issue with chairman of the Securities and Investments Board, Sir Andrew Large, the lead regulator for the LME. He will ask about a statement by King at the American Metal Markets conference when he knew the copper price was being kept artificially high by Sumitomo's chief trader Hamanaka.
-- BARINGS CHIEFS FACE BAN AS DIRECTORS

Former deputy chairman of Barings, Andrew Tuckey, and nine other senior executives in charge at the merchant bank when it crashed will face disqualification from the Department of Trade and Industry as company directors for up to 15 years. The DTI is to use the Company Directors Disqualification Act of 1986. The 10 directors have already been investigated by the Securities and Futures Authority, however, Tuckey did not face disciplinary action.
-- US UTILITY SET TO BID FOR YORKSHIRE ELECTRICITY

American Electric Power, a US utility, has approached Yorkshire Electricity towards a 1.4 billion stg bid. This will leave only one of the 14 regional electricity companies independent. The bid could create a 2.5 billion stg windfall for the Yorkshire directors, with chief executive Malcolm Chatwin as the main beneficiary. The Americans may pull out of a deal if the electricity regulator, Stephen Littlechild, forces a referral to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
THE GUARDIAN
-- TORY JOBS CLAIM IS FALSE, SAYS REPORT

According to the Employment Policy Institute, the Government's claim that it has cut unemployment by a third since recession is false. The report claims that unemployment has dropped below two million as a result of structural changes in the economy and not Tory-instigated deregulation of the labour market. The report also attacks the Government's claim that Britain's job record has made it the envy of other European countries.
-- TUC SAYS UNIONS MUST RECRUIT ANOTHER HALF-MILLION MEMBERS JUST TO STAND STILL

The TUC has warned that if unions are to halt a long-term slide they will have to step up organising campaigns to recruit an extra half-a-million members by the end of the millennium. The TUC has told its constituent unions to target "new" workers, from white-collar professionals to those employed in so called "McJobs", particularly women part-timers. Between 1989 and 1995 union membership fell by 1.7 million to 7.3 million.
-- NATWEST TO GO SHARE SHOPPING

National Westminster Bank is expected to announce plans for repurchase of 225 million stg worth of shares, as well as an eight percent rise in profit to 1.89 billion stg for the first half of its year. The bank has repurchased 450 million stg worth of shares in August and has received authorisation from shareholders to buy back a further 28 million units. The trading picture could be good because the domestic economy has been strong and costs have continued to fall.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- 'WINDFALLS WILL BE SAVED NOT SPENT'

According to a survey by Mori and analysis by Salomon Brothers, only one in eight of the 19 million recipients of the 21 billion stg worth of shares to be given away by the converting building societies will cash in their shares straightaway. This will have the effect of subduing the "feel-good factor" and easing the pressure on Chancellor Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates. The survey suggests the windfalls will be saved rather than spent and add 0.5 percent to consumption rates.
-- SCARDINO PULLS OUT OF FOREST BID BATTLE

A 20 million stg bid by a consortium led by US journalist Albert Scardino for Nottingham Forest has collapsed due to Mercury Asset Management, his main backer pulling out. MAM said it was to withdraw because of the possible deterioration of the market for football shares over the next 18 months, a decision that could have a knock-on effect on other quoted football clubs. Scardino was unsuccessful to bring in replacement backers.
-- ORANGE TARGETS BIG-SPENDING BUSINESS TRAVELLERS WITH GLOBALLY MOBILE PHONE

Orange is to offer a mobile phone which can be used in more than 50 countries by the end of this year. The new phones have been developed with Motorola and will allow calls to be made on either of the two main types of digital network in common use and are claimed to be the basis of the first international phone network. Orange claims it will have a lead of three to four months on its competitors in introducing the duel-mode technology, which searches out the correct frequency automatically.
